relevance_reason: The title describes the clinical, biochemical and molecular features of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency and long-term follow-up of nine patients. Only the title was available, so no specific details could be extracted.

findings.statement: Chapel-Crespo et al. (2019) reported the clinical, biochemical and molecular characteristics of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, with long-term follow-up of 9 patients.
quotes: Clinical, biochemical and molecular characteristics of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency and long-term follow-up of nine patients.

relevance_reason: Case report of a patient with MCD deficiency describing brain malformations and MLYCD molecular findings.

findings.statement: de Wit et al. (2006) described a girl with MCD deficiency whose brain MRI showed white matter abnormalities together with diffuse pachygyria and periventricular heterotopia, consistent with a malformation of cortical development. The patient had strikingly low appetite, which the authors noted was interesting in light of the proposed role of malonyl-CoA in feeding control, but which remained to be confirmed in other patients.
quotes: We describe a girl with MCD deficiency, whose brain MRI shows white matter abnormalities and additionally diffuse pachygyria and periventricular heterotopia, consistent with a malformation of cortical development.
Our patient has strikingly low appetite, which is interesting in the light of the proposed role of malonyl-CoA in the regulation of feeding control

findings.statement: In the girl with MCD deficiency, de Wit et al. (2006) found a normal MLYCD genomic sequence but no MLYCD messenger product, suggesting an abnormality of transcription regulation.
quotes: MLYCD-gene sequence analysis shows normal genomic sequence but no messenger product, suggesting an abnormality of transcription regulation.

findings.statement: de Wit et al. (2006) recommended that patients with MCD deficiency be evaluated with brain MRI and that unexplained malformations of cortical development prompt metabolic screening.
quotes: patients with MCD deficiency should be evaluated with brain MRI and unexplained malformations of cortical development should be reason for metabolic screening.

relevance_reason: The paper reports MLYCD mutation analysis in patients with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, with functional studies of protein level and localization.

findings.statement: Wightman et al. (2003) described malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MLYCD) deficiency as an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by malonic aciduria, developmental delay, seizures, hypoglycemia, and cardiomyopathy.
quotes: Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MLYCD) deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by malonic aciduria, developmental delay, seizure disorder, hypoglycemia, and cardiomyopathy.

findings.statement: Wightman et al. (2003) sequenced the genomic MLYCD gene in 9 unrelated patients with MLYCD deficiency and identified 16 of 18 pathogenic alleles. They recorded these variants in a newly created Human MLYCD Allelic Variant Database.
quotes: Genomic sequencing of MLYCD in nine unrelated patients identified 16 of 18 pathogenic alleles, which are documented in the newly created Human MLYCD Allelic Variant Database

findings.statement: Wightman et al. (2003) carried out Western blot analysis on fibroblast cell lines from 8 of their patients and 2 previously reported patients with homozygous MLYCD mutations. The 66-kDa MLYCD band was absent in 6 patients and substantially reduced in 3. One patient had increased protein levels, with a prominent smeary band at 68 to 83 kDa.
quotes: Fibroblast cell lines were available from eight of these patients and two previously reported patients with homozygous MLYCD mutations.
Western blot analysis using antisera raised to a C-terminal peptide detected a 66-kDa band that was absent in six patients and substantially reduced in three patients.
One patient showed an increase in protein levels with a prominent smeary 68-l83-kDa band.

findings.statement: Wightman et al. (2003) identified an extreme N-terminal MLYCD mutation, c.8G>A (p.G3D), in a patient with MLYCD deficiency. On immunocytochemistry, the mutant protein mislocalized to the plasma membrane. The authors suggested that a novel targeting signal may reside in a conserved 4-amino acid N-terminal motif.
quotes: An extreme N-terminal mutation c.8G>A (p.G3D) mislocalized to the plasma membrane, suggesting that a novel targeting signal may reside in a four-amino acid conserved N-terminal motif.

findings.statement: Wightman et al. (2003) identified a point mutation, c.119T>C (p.M40T), in a patient with MLYCD deficiency. This mutation ablates the second of the putative mitochondrial and peroxisomal initiating codons (M40). On immunocytochemistry, the mutant protein showed punctate perinuclear staining.
quotes: A 25-base deletion between the putative mitochondrial and peroxisomal initiating codons (M1 and M40) and a point mutation ablating the second of these (c.119T>C, p.M40T) both showed punctate perinuclear staining.

findings.statement: Wightman et al. (2003) identified a 25-base deletion in MLYCD, located between the putative mitochondrial (M1) and peroxisomal (M40) initiating codons, in a patient with MLYCD deficiency. On immunocytochemistry, the mutant protein showed punctate perinuclear staining.
quotes: A 25-base deletion between the putative mitochondrial and peroxisomal initiating codons (M1 and M40) and a point mutation ablating the second of these (c.119T>C, p.M40T) both showed punctate perinuclear staining.

findings.statement: Wightman et al. (2003) found apparent intracellular mislocalization of MLYCD in patient cell lines that still expressed the protein. None of the 3 mislocalizing mutations was predicted to alter catalytic function, so the authors concluded that correct subcellular localization of MLYCD is likely critical for normal function.
quotes: Immunocytochemical analysis of MLYCD-expressing patient cell lines showed apparent intracellular mislocalization.

As none of the three mislocalizing mutations are predicted to alter the catalytic function of the peptide, it seems likely that correct subcellular localization of MLYCD is critical for it to function normally.

relevance_reason: This paper identifies MCD as the gene for human malonyl-CoA decarboxylase and reports a mutation in the gene in a patient with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency.

findings.statement: Sacksteder et al. (1999) described malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency as a lethal disorder characterized by cardiomyopathy and developmental delay, associated with defects in MCD activity. MCD catalyzes the proton-consuming conversion of malonyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA and CO2.
quotes: Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MCD) catalyzes the proton-consuming conversion of malonyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA and CO(2).
defects in MCD activity are associated with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, a lethal disorder characterized by cardiomyopathy and developmental delay

findings.statement: In a patient with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, Sacksteder et al. (1999) identified a severe mutation in the MCD gene, a 2-bp deletion (c.947-948delTT). They had found MCD in a computer-based search for new peroxisomal proteins. Together with the high malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity of the recombinant protein, the mutation confirmed that the gene encodes human MCD.
quotes: a malonyl-CoA decarboxylase-deficient patient has a severe mutation in the MCD gene (c.947-948delTT), confirming that this gene encodes human MCD

findings.statement: Sacksteder et al. (1999) found that recombinant MCD protein had high intrinsic malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity. The protein carries a canonical type-1 peroxisomal targeting signal (serine-lysine-leucine at the C terminus). Subcellular fractionation showed that MCD is located in both the cytoplasm and peroxisomes.
quotes: which encodes a protein with a canonical type-1 peroxisomal targeting signal of serine-lysine-leucine(COOH)
We observed that recombinant MCD protein has high intrinsic malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity
Subcellular fractionation experiments revealed that MCD resides in both the cytoplasm and peroxisomes.

findings.statement: Sacksteder et al. (1999) proposed that cytoplasmic MCD regulates the amount of cytoplasmic malonyl-CoA and, through it, mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and oxidation. They noted that MCD mRNA is most abundant in cardiac and skeletal muscle, and that patients have phenotypes reminiscent of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation disorders. They also suggested that peroxisomal MCD may degrade intraperoxisomal malonyl-CoA produced by beta-oxidation of odd chain-length dicarboxylic fatty acids.
quotes: Cytoplasmic MCD is positioned to play a role in the regulation of cytoplasmic malonyl-CoA abundance and, thus, of mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and oxidation.
malonyl-CoA decarboxylase-deficient patients display a number of phenotypes that are reminiscent of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation disorders
MCD mRNA is most abundant in cardiac and skeletal muscles

relevance_reason: Identifies the first causative MCD mutations in patients with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency.

findings.statement: FitzPatrick et al. (1999) identified a homozygous 442C-G transversion in the MCD gene, producing a premature stop codon (S148X) in the N-terminal half of the protein, in fibroblast RNA from one of two previously reported consanguineous Scottish patients with MCD deficiency. They found it by RT-PCR analysis. The mutation segregated appropriately within the family and was not present in 100 normal unrelated individuals.
quotes: We have identified two different homozygous mutations in human MCD (hMCD) by using RT-PCR analysis of fibroblast RNA from two previously reported consanguineous Scottish patients with MCD deficiency.
The first mutation is a 442C-->G transversion resulting in a premature stop codon (S148X) in the N-terminal half of the protein.
Both mutations were found to segregate appropriately within the families and were not found in 100 normal unrelated individuals.

findings.statement: In the second consanguineous Scottish patient with MCD deficiency, FitzPatrick et al. (1999) found a homozygous intronic mutation in the MCD gene (IVS4-14A-G). It created a novel splice acceptor site, which led to a 13-bp insertion in the mature RNA, a frameshift, and predicted truncation of the protein. The mutation segregated appropriately within the family and was absent from 100 normal unrelated controls.
quotes: The second is a 13-bp insertion in the mature RNA, causing a frameshift with predicted protein truncation.
This insertion is the result of an intronic mutation generating a novel splice acceptor sequence (IVS4-14A-->G).
Both mutations were found to segregate appropriately within the families and were not found in 100 normal unrelated individuals.

findings.statement: FitzPatrick et al. (1999) found homozygous MCD mutations in two patients with MCD deficiency from consanguineous Scottish families, which is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
quotes: We have identified two different homozygous mutations in human MCD (hMCD) by using RT-PCR analysis of fibroblast RNA from two previously reported consanguineous Scottish patients with MCD deficiency.

findings.statement: FitzPatrick et al. (1999) found that the human MCD peptide carries a C-terminal peroxisomal targeting sequence (-SKL). In rat liver homogenates, subcellular fractionation showed a distribution of MCD enzyme activity that strongly suggested MCD is located in peroxisomes as well as mitochondria.
quotes: The peptide sequence of hMCD revealed a C-terminal peroxisomal targeting sequence (-SKL).

the distribution of MCD enzymatic activity in rat liver homogenates-as measured by means of subcellular fractionation-strongly suggests that MCD is localized to peroxisomes in addition to the mitochondrial localization reported elsewhere.

relevance_reason: The paper reports cloning the human MCD gene and finding the mutation that causes malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency in a patient.

findings.statement: Gao et al. (1999) noted that malonyl-CoA decarboxylase converts malonyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA. They stated that deficiency of the enzyme has been associated with mild mental retardation, seizures, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, vomiting, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and malonic aciduria.
quotes: Malonyl coenzyme A (CoA) decarboxylase (E.C.4. 1.1.9) catalyzes the conversion of malonyl CoA to acetyl CoA.
deficiency of the enzyme has been associated with mild mental retardation, seizures, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, vomiting, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and malonic aciduria

findings.statement: Gao et al. (1999) found the mutation underlying malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency in a patient who had clinical features of the defect, malonic aciduria, and markedly reduced malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity. The abstract does not name the mutation. The authors identified the human MCD gene by its homology to the goose gene.
quotes: The genetic mutation underlying malonyl CoA decarboxylase deficiency was determined in a patient with clinical features of this defect, malonic aciduria, and markedly reduced malonyl CoA decarboxylase activity.
Here we report the isolation and sequencing of the human gene encoding malonyl CoA decarboxylase, and the identification of a mutation causing malonyl CoA decarboxylase deficiency.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Abnormal circulating enzyme concentration or activity

findings.statement: Gao et al. (1999) identified the human malonyl-CoA decarboxylase cDNA by its homology to the goose gene. The 1,479-bp human cDNA is 70% identical to the goose sequence. The intron/exon boundaries, which they determined by sequencing a PAC clone, are completely conserved between the two species.
quotes: The 1479 basepair human cDNA is 70 percent identical to the goose sequence, and the intron/exon boundaries are completely conserved between the two species.

relevance_reason: Reports two new patients with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, including clinical and biochemical findings.

findings.statement: MacPhee et al. (1993) described 2 Scottish-born children with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency whose consanguineous parents were of Scots/Irish origin. The children were investigated during episodes of vomiting and febrile convulsions, along with developmental delay. Before this report, the disorder had been reported in only 2 Australian children.
quotes: The new cases are Scots born and are the offspring of consanguinous parents of Scots/Irish origin.
They were investigated during episodes of vomiting and febrile convulsions associated with concomitant developmental delay.
Hitherto, the worldwide experience of the disorder has been confined to reports on two affected Australian children.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Febrile seizure (within the age range of 3 months to 6 years)

findings.statement: MacPhee et al. (1993) found malonic aciduria and greatly reduced malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity in 2 Scottish patients. They presented urinary organic acid profiles obtained by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and compared the clinical and biochemical features of these patients with those of the Australian patients.
quotes: Malonic aciduria and grossly reduced malonyl CoA decarboxylase activity were demonstrated and the total ion current chromatograms of urinary organic acid profiles obtained by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry are presented.

relevance_reason: This is the first report of a patient with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, an inborn error of metabolism that had not been recognized before.

findings.statement: Brown et al. (1984) described a child with deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme malonyl-CoA decarboxylase, an inborn error of metabolism that had not been recognized before. The child had repeated episodes of vomiting, some of which required hospitalization.
quotes: A patient is described with a deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme, malonyl CoA decarboxylase - an inborn error of metabolism not recognized previously.
in a child with repeated episodes of vomiting, some requiring hospitalization

findings.statement: Brown et al. (1984) first suspected malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency in their patient because the child persistently excreted malonic and methylmalonic acids in the urine. The authors also demonstrated disturbances of lipid metabolism.
quotes: The enzyme defect was first suspected because of persistent excretion of malonic and methylmalonic acids in urine
Disturbances of lipid metabolism were demonstrated.

relevance_reason: Case report of a second patient with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, giving clinical, biochemical, enzymatic and dietary-response data.

findings.statement: Haan et al. (1986) described a boy, the second reported child with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, whose enzyme defect was more severe. He was mildly mentally retarded. During a urinary tract infection he presented with vomiting, a seizure, hypoglycemia and mild metabolic acidosis.
quotes: A second child with a more severe deficiency of malonyl CoA decarboxylase is described.
He is mildly mentally retarded and presented with vomiting, a seizure, hypoglycaemia and mild metabolic acidosis during a urinary tract infection.

findings.statement: Haan et al. (1986) found that the patient's urine contained increased amounts of malonic, methylmalonic, succinic, adipic, glutaric and suberic acids. Mitochondrial malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity in extracts of his cultured fibroblasts was 4% of the mean control value.
quotes: The urine contained increased amounts of malonic, methylmalonic, succinic, adipic, glutaric and suberic acids.
Mitochondrial malonyl CoA decarboxylase activity in cultured fibroblast extracts was 4% of the mean control value.

findings.statement: Haan et al. (1986) found that a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet led to symptomatic hypoglycemia, moderate metabolic acidosis, and excretion of large amounts of the same organic acids and 3-hydroxybutyrate in the urine. On an isocaloric low-fat, high-carbohydrate diet, only relatively small quantities of malonic, methylmalonic and succinic acids were excreted. Acute fat and lysine loads increased urinary malonic acid excretion without affecting excretion of the other organic acids.
quotes: A high fat, low carbohydrate diet led to symptomatic hypoglycaemia, a moderate metabolic acidosis and excretion in the urine of large amounts of the same organic acids and 3-hydroxybutyrate.
Only relatively small quantities of malonic, methylmalonic and succinic acid were excreted in the urine when the boy was fed an isocaloric low fat, high carbohydrate diet.
Acute fat and lysine loads led to increased excretion of malonic acid in the urine without affecting the excretion of the other organic acids.

findings.statement: Haan et al. (1986) suggested that malonyl-CoA decarboxylase serves an important function in the mitochondrion by preventing accumulation of malonyl-CoA, and that its importance is best seen when fat is the main metabolic fuel. They noted that the mechanisms by which malonyl-CoA produces its complex metabolic effects remained to be elucidated.
quotes: Experience with this patient suggests that malonyl CoA decarboxylase serves an important function in the mitochondrion by preventing accumulation of malonyl CoA.
The importance of the enzyme is best seen when fat is the main metabolic fuel.
